paras: The lynching of George Betts and James Browning was the hanging of two men accused of killing Sheriff E. N. Campbell, carried out by masked men who took them from the jail at Lake City, Colorado, early on April 27, 1882. The two were hanged from a bridge over the Gunnison River about a day after the sheriff was shot. Telegraph dispatches carried the story nationally within a day, and weeklies listed it among the week's lynchings.

According to a Lake City dispatch to the Denver Times dated April 26, Sheriff Campbell was shot through the heart about two o'clock that morning while guarding the contents of a vacant house against thieves. The dispatch blamed "two low dance house men," George Betts and James Browning, and added that a lynching was "apprehended to-night." The Ottawa Free Trader said the pair kept "a low drinking and gambling den" and that Belts fired when Campbell, watching a burgled storehouse with an assistant named Smith, ordered them to throw up their hands.
Both were arrested that morning and jailed under guard; the Ottawa paper said a coroner's jury had placed their guilt "beyond a doubt."

At about one o'clock on the morning of April 27, according to the wire report, about 100 masked men overpowered the guard at the jail and took out the two prisoners. The Elk Mountain Pilot reported that they broke open the doors and led the prisoners with ropes around their necks to the Ocean Wave bridge across the Gunnison River, "in the lower part of town" by the wire account. Betts was said to have asked for a chew of tobacco, and the Pilot added that his last request was that his body be turned over to his wife.

According to Hickman, the Lake City land-office receiver, speaking to the Denver Tribune, the crowd gathered at the dead sheriff's house in answer to a rumored "prayer-meeting" called for eleven o'clock. Some wanted to spare Browning as not the shooter, he said, but Browning was hanged after threatening revenge on the witnesses. Campbell's brothers arrived from Pitkin as the men were being pulled up.

The bodies were left hanging under guard until nine the next morning, or until late in the day according to Hickman. The Ottawa Free Trader said officers then cut them down and buried them, and Hickman said they were buried before the sheriff's funeral. No report of an inquest or of any arrest of the lynchers appears in the coverage. Asked whether anyone objected, Hickman said "the people all thought the act a good one."

The story first ran as two wire items: the April 26 report of the shooting, in the Cheyenne Daily Leader and the Sacramento Daily Record-Union, and the lynching dispatch, printed April 27 in the Alexandria Gazette, the Memphis Public Ledger, the Sacramento paper and the Press and Daily Dakotaian. Headlines were plain: "Lynched," "Judge Lynch," "Two Men Launched by Lynchers." The wire text stated the accusation as fact, saying the two "shot and killed Sheriff Campbell," and praised their composure with "Both died game."

Over the next week, weeklies from Kentucky to Wisconsin condensed it into crime digests beside other lynchings of the same day. The Bourbon News and the Somerset Press closed one such paragraph with "A good record for one day," and the Eaton Democrat misplaced Lake City in California.

In June the Denver Tribune's interview with Hickman, headed "Lynch Law in Colorado," was reprinted in the Iron County Register and in the Centre Democrat, which added the headline "How a Prayer-Meeting Went Down the Street." None of the reports described the race of either man.

Wire copies named the second man "Jim Brown," while the first dispatch, the Pilot, the Ottawa paper and Hickman used Browning, and the first man's name was also printed Belts, Bolts and Betta. The crowd was put at 100 men by the wire, the Pilot and Hickman, but at 70 by the Ottawa Free Trader. Hickman's account put the hanging a day later than the dated dispatches and the Pilot, which were written closer to the event and give April 27. The wire said both "died game," while another version said they "died making no remark of any kind."

bases: A crowd of about 100 masked men took two men accused of killing a sheriff from the Lake City jail and hanged them from a bridge (A4, A19, A25, A27).

Two jailed men were taken by 70 to 100 masked men who overpowered the guard and hanged them for the killing of Sheriff Campbell, with no legal authority (A4, A19, A25); Hickman described the crowd as demanding 'eye for an eye' (A27). No report gives the victims' race.

The wire report, the Colorado Elk Mountain Pilot, the Ottawa Free Trader and the Hickman interview independently agree on the jail seizure and hanging from a Gunnison River bridge (A4, A19, A25, A27).

Weekly digests listed it among the day's lynchings with the ironic 'A good record for one day.'
The Hickman interview called it the boldest lynching on the frontier and reported local approval.
